items.prompt: A general-purpose SSD workload needs more IOPS but not more capacity. Which EBS option provides independent performance tuning?
constraints: The workload is attached to EC2.
Capacity is adequate.
IOPS is the measured bottleneck.

options.text: Use gp3 and provision the required IOPS independently from volume size, then validate the instance bandwidth limit.
Increase gp2 size only because gp3 IOPS is fixed by capacity.
Use sc1 because all SSD-like workloads are throughput workloads.
Use instance store because it is always durable.

feedback.Reason: gp3 lets the architect tune IOPS and throughput separately from capacity within its service limits.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: gp3 provides baseline performance and separately configurable IOPS and throughput, while EC2 still limits the path.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner sizes the volume for data and provisions only the performance the measured workload requires.
Details.errorCorrection: gp2 performance is linked to size, sc1 is HDD throughput storage, and instance store is ephemeral.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Provisioned performance adds cost and cannot exceed instance or volume limits.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: gp2 ties performance more closely to size and does not offer gp3's independent model.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: sc1 is not an SSD choice for random IOPS.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Instance store data is not durable across instance failure or stop behavior.

items.prompt: A database requires sustained high IOPS, low latency, and a higher durability target than a general-purpose development volume. Which choice should be evaluated?
constraints: IOPS is consistently high.
Data is business-critical.
The application uses EBS block semantics.

options.text: Evaluate io2 or an appropriate provisioned-IOPS SSD, sizing IOPS, throughput, durability, and instance bandwidth from measured requirements.
Use sc1 because high IOPS databases need the cheapest volume.
Use gp3 without checking whether its maximum IOPS meets the workload.
Use instance store and rebuild the database after every failure.

feedback.Reason: Provisioned-IOPS SSD options fit sustained high-IOPS, low-latency database workloads and should be sized with the complete path.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: io2 is designed for provisioned IOPS and higher durability characteristics than general-purpose SSD options.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect validates engine I/O, queueing, volume limits, and instance bandwidth before selecting a performance and durability tier.
Details.errorCorrection: sc1 is throughput HDD, gp3 may not meet high IOPS without checking limits, and instance store is not a durable database foundation.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Provisioned IOPS costs more and should be justified by sustained demand and business impact.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: sc1 is designed for throughput-oriented cold data, not high random IOPS.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A general-purpose choice must still meet measured maximum IOPS and latency.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Rebuilding from failure does not provide the required durability or recovery time.

items.prompt: A log-processing workload performs large sequential reads and writes and is not latency-sensitive. Which EBS family is a candidate?
constraints: Access is sequential.
Throughput matters more than random IOPS.
The data is reproducible or separately protected.

options.text: Evaluate a throughput-optimized HDD such as st1, sizing throughput, capacity, workload duration, and recovery needs.
Use io2 solely because every workload should maximize IOPS.
Use instance store as the durable source of logs.
Use sc1 for a continuously active high-throughput workload without testing its limits.

feedback.Reason: st1 targets throughput-intensive workloads where sequential access matters more than random IOPS.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Throughput-optimized HDD volumes are designed for large sequential workloads and have workload and size limits.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner benchmarks sustained throughput and keeps separate backup or regeneration protection for the logs.
Details.errorCorrection: io2 can overpay for a throughput workload, instance store is ephemeral, and sc1 is for colder infrequent throughput patterns.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: HDD throughput varies with workload and may not fit latency-sensitive or random I/O.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Maximum IOPS is not the same as best fit for sequential throughput.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Instance store is not durable source-of-truth storage.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: sc1 is not the usual choice for continuously active throughput-intensive data.

items.prompt: A large dataset is accessed infrequently but when accessed needs economical sequential throughput. Which volume should be compared?
constraints: Access is infrequent.
The workload is sequential.
Latency can be higher than SSD.

options.text: Compare sc1 with other storage options using access frequency, throughput, capacity, restore time, and data-protection requirements.
Use io2 because cold data must have maximum random IOPS.
Use gp3 without considering idle storage cost or throughput needs.
Use instance store because infrequently accessed data is safe to lose.

feedback.Reason: sc1 is a candidate for cold, throughput-oriented HDD data when its latency and durability trade-offs fit.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Cold HDD volumes target infrequent access and large sequential throughput rather than high random IOPS.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner validates restore and access time, backup, capacity, and whether a different service or archive tier is more appropriate.
Details.errorCorrection: io2 overprovisions random performance, gp3 may cost more for idle data, and instance store is ephemeral.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Cold HDD has lower performance and availability characteristics than active SSD choices and must match the workload.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: High provisioned IOPS is not required for infrequent sequential access.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: General-purpose SSD can be uneconomic for cold capacity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Infrequent access does not mean data can be lost.

items.prompt: A gp2 volume performs well during short bursts but slows during sustained load after burst credits are depleted. What should the team evaluate?
constraints: The workload has sustained I/O periods.
The volume type can be changed.
Performance needs to be predictable.

options.text: Measure sustained demand and compare gp3 or another volume type that provides the required predictable IOPS and throughput without relying on burst credits.
Increase application concurrency so credits replenish faster.
Assume burst performance is the sustained guarantee.
Delete snapshots to replenish volume performance credits.

feedback.Reason: Burst behavior is not a substitute for a sustained performance requirement.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Some volume models use burst or baseline performance, while gp3 allows explicit IOPS and throughput configuration.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner measures the demand window, chooses a predictable type, and validates the migration and performance result.
Details.errorCorrection: More concurrency consumes credits faster, burst is not sustained guarantee, and snapshots do not control volume credits.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Predictable provisioned performance can increase cost and still remains bounded by instance bandwidth.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: More load accelerates credit depletion.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Burst performance cannot be treated as a sustained guarantee.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Snapshot operations do not replenish performance credits.

items.prompt: A workload is limited by bytes per second rather than operations per second. Which EBS configuration question is most important?
constraints: I/O sizes are large.
Throughput is the measured bottleneck.
The instance path is finite.

options.text: Choose and provision throughput from measured I/O size and concurrency, then verify the volume and EC2 instance throughput limits.
Provision the maximum IOPS and ignore MiB/s.
Choose a volume solely from capacity in GiB.
Use a smaller I/O size without checking application behavior.

feedback.Reason: Large I/O workloads can be throughput-bound even when IOPS is low.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Throughput is a function of I/O size and rate and is bounded separately at volume and instance levels.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect benchmarks actual I/O, provisions throughput, and checks queueing and instance EBS bandwidth.
Details.errorCorrection: IOPS alone ignores byte rate, capacity does not define throughput, and changing I/O size can change application behavior.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Higher throughput may cost more and can move the bottleneck to network or compute.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: High IOPS does not necessarily provide the required byte throughput.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Capacity is distinct from performance.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: I/O size is a workload property and should not be changed blindly.

items.prompt: An EBS volume meets its provisioned IOPS but the application sees lower performance on a non-EBS-optimized instance. What is the correction?
constraints: The volume type is appropriate.
The instance exposes a finite storage path.
The workload needs predictable I/O.

options.text: Use an EBS-optimized or otherwise compatible instance with sufficient EBS bandwidth and validate the complete volume-to-instance path.
Increase volume IOPS without changing the instance path.
Put the volume in another Availability Zone to increase bandwidth.
Disable EBS monitoring so the instance can use more bandwidth.

feedback.Reason: The instance's storage path can cap EBS performance even when the volume is provisioned correctly.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EBS-optimized instances provide dedicated or specified bandwidth for EBS traffic and have their own limits.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner selects a compatible instance, measures queue depth and throughput, and validates cost and compute fit.
Details.errorCorrection: More volume IOPS cannot bypass an instance cap, AZ movement does not increase instance bandwidth, and monitoring does not consume the path in that way.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A larger instance may add cost and compute capacity beyond the storage need.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: The instance remains the limiting boundary.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: An AZ change does not change the instance's EBS bandwidth capability.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Monitoring is needed to diagnose the path and is not the cause of the limit.

items.prompt: A gp3 volume needs more IOPS while the application remains online. Which option should be considered?
constraints: The volume type supports modification.
The application cannot stop for a long window.
The change must be monitored.

options.text: Use Elastic Volumes to modify supported volume attributes online, monitor modification state and performance, and plan a fallback if the target is not met.
Detach the volume during every performance change regardless of service support.
Delete and recreate the volume without a backup.
Increase IOPS in the application without changing storage.

feedback.Reason: Elastic Volumes can change supported EBS attributes without the traditional detach-and-recreate path.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EBS volume modification supports changing type, size, and performance attributes for supported volumes while attached, with a transition state.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner checks support, starts the modification, observes completion and metrics, and validates application performance.
Details.errorCorrection: Unnecessary detachment adds downtime, deletion risks data, and application settings cannot create storage IOPS.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Modification takes time and may have limits, so changes need capacity and rollback planning.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Detachment may be unnecessary and creates avoidable downtime.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Recreation without backup is destructive.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Application concurrency is not provisioned EBS performance.

items.prompt: A restored EBS volume shows lower performance until blocks are read. What should the recovery design account for?
constraints: The volume was restored from a snapshot.
The application has an RTO.
Warm-up can be planned.

options.text: Account for snapshot restore initialization, pre-warm or read required blocks when supported, and include the warm-up time in recovery testing.
Assume snapshot completion means every block is immediately at production performance.
Delete the snapshot after volume creation to speed up reads.
Increase DNS TTL to accelerate block initialization.

feedback.Reason: Snapshot-created volumes can have initialization behavior that affects time-to-performance and RTO.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Blocks may be initialized on first access or through an explicit fast restore or initialization mechanism depending on the volume and workflow.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner restores in advance or reads required data, measures application latency, and includes this phase in recovery capacity.
Details.errorCorrection: Snapshot availability is not identical to warmed performance, deletion does not initialize blocks, and DNS is unrelated.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Pre-initialization consumes I/O and time and must be balanced against recovery load.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Snapshot restoration and performance initialization can be distinct phases.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Deleting a snapshot does not warm volume blocks.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: DNS caching cannot affect block initialization.

items.prompt: A single volume cannot provide the measured IOPS required by a striped application that can tolerate multiple volumes. What should be evaluated?
constraints: The application can stripe data.
Failure of one member must be handled.
The performance target is measured.

options.text: Evaluate a supported software RAID or application striping design, including aggregate throughput, failure handling, rebuild, backups, and operational complexity.
Stripe volumes without a recovery plan because more devices always improve availability.
Use instance store and call it EBS RAID.
Create more volumes without changing the application or filesystem.

feedback.Reason: Striping can increase aggregate performance but changes failure and recovery behavior and must be treated as a complete design.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Multiple EBS volumes can provide parallel paths when the application or filesystem supports it, but one member failure can affect the array.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner benchmarks aggregate limits, snapshots or backups, rebuild time, and degraded behavior before deployment.
Details.errorCorrection: More devices can increase failure surface, instance store is different storage, and unused volumes do not aggregate performance automatically.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Striping adds management and recovery complexity and may reduce fault tolerance without mirroring or backups.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Striping without failure and backup design can reduce availability.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Instance store is not EBS and has different persistence behavior.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Additional volumes do not help unless the software uses them.

items.prompt: An EBS workload reports high queue depth and rising latency while requested IOPS remain below provisioned maximum. What should be investigated?
constraints: Latency is measured at the application.
I/O size and concurrency are known.
The volume and instance have separate limits.

options.text: Correlate queue depth, I/O size, latency, volume and instance throughput, filesystem behavior, and application concurrency before changing the volume type.
Increase IOPS blindly because queue depth always means insufficient IOPS.
Delete queued operations to lower the metric.
Use a larger capacity volume without measuring performance limits.

feedback.Reason: Queueing can arise from I/O size, throughput, instance, filesystem, or application concurrency and is not automatically an IOPS shortage.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EBS metrics need to be interpreted with request size and the complete host-to-volume path.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner isolates the bottleneck and then selects IOPS, throughput, instance, filesystem, or application tuning.
Details.errorCorrection: Blind IOPS increases can miss a throughput or client limit, deleting work is unsafe, and capacity size is not a performance diagnosis.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Deep diagnosis takes time but prevents expensive changes that leave latency unresolved.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Queue depth has multiple possible causes and does not prove an IOPS deficit.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Deleting queued operations loses work and hides the problem.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Capacity and performance are separate dimensions.

items.prompt: A clustered application needs multiple instances to access the same block volume. What must be verified before using EBS Multi-Attach?
constraints: The volume and instance types support the feature.
The application or filesystem is cluster-aware.
Data corruption is unacceptable.

options.text: Verify supported volume and instance requirements and use a cluster-aware filesystem or application that coordinates concurrent block access; do not treat Multi-Attach as a generic shared disk.
Attach any volume to any instances and let ordinary filesystems coordinate writes.
Use Multi-Attach to share a boot volume across Regions.
Assume multiple attachments automatically provide replication.

feedback.Reason: Multi-Attach changes the attachment topology but does not provide generic filesystem locking or replication.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Supported io1 or io2 configurations can attach to multiple instances in an AZ, but concurrent block access needs cluster coordination.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect validates the cluster software, failure handling, snapshots, and AZ scope before adopting the feature.
Details.errorCorrection: Ordinary filesystems can corrupt data, boot volumes and Regions have separate limits, and attachment is not replication.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Multi-Attach increases coordination and failure complexity and may not be the right shared-file model.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Generic filesystems do not automatically coordinate multi-writer block access.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Multi-Attach has specific scope and is not cross-Region boot sharing.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Multiple attachments do not create independent data copies.

items.prompt: A team selects encrypted EBS volumes for sensitive data and worries that encryption removes all performance capability. What is the correct design stance?
constraints: Data must be encrypted at rest.
The workload has a performance target.
The service supports encrypted EBS.

options.text: Use encrypted EBS with appropriate KMS permissions and benchmark the actual volume and instance path; encryption is a security control, not a reason to skip performance validation.
Disable encryption because performance always requires plaintext volumes.
Encrypt only the filesystem metadata and leave blocks plaintext.
Use S3 encryption as a substitute for the attached block volume's encryption.

feedback.Reason: EBS encryption protects volume data and can be used with performance-oriented volume choices; the complete path still needs measurement.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Encrypted EBS uses KMS and service-managed data-key handling while exposing the same block-storage model to the instance.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner grants least-privilege key access, creates encrypted snapshots or volumes, and benchmarks the chosen type.
Details.errorCorrection: Plaintext storage violates the requirement, partial encryption is insufficient, and S3 encryption does not encrypt an EBS block device.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Key permissions and KMS availability become dependencies for create, attach, and recovery operations.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Encryption is required and supported for EBS workloads.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Protecting only metadata leaves data blocks exposed.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: S3 controls do not protect EBS volume blocks.

items.prompt: A team doubles an EBS volume size to gain performance, but the application needed more throughput with the same capacity. What should be corrected?
constraints: Data capacity is sufficient.
Throughput is measured.
The volume type supports independent performance settings.

options.text: Select a volume and performance configuration from measured IOPS or throughput needs; do not increase capacity as a proxy when the service supports independent tuning.
Keep doubling capacity because capacity and performance are always identical.
Delete the volume and recreate it with no snapshot.
Use a larger filesystem block size without measuring the application.

feedback.Reason: Capacity and performance are related differently by volume type; sizing should follow the actual bottleneck.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: gp3 and provisioned performance options can separate capacity from IOPS or throughput within limits.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner chooses capacity for data and performance settings for measured access, then validates cost and instance bandwidth.
Details.errorCorrection: Doubling capacity can overpay and still miss throughput, deletion loses data, and filesystem changes can affect correctness.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Independent provisioning does not remove service or instance limits.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: The relationship is volume-type-specific and is not always one-to-one.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Recreation without a protected copy is destructive.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Filesystem block size is not a universal throughput control.

items.prompt: Which metrics best indicate that an EBS workload is approaching its performance boundary?
constraints: The application has latency objectives.
The volume and instance expose metrics.
The team needs leading indicators.

options.text: Correlate volume read and write latency, queueing, operations, throughput, burst or credit state where relevant, instance EBS limits, and application latency.
Monitor only volume size.
Use database row count as the storage performance metric.
Alarm only after the application times out.

feedback.Reason: Performance boundaries are multi-layer and should be detected before customer timeouts.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: CloudWatch EBS metrics and application latency together reveal volume, instance, and workload saturation.
Details.scenarioApplication: Operators alarm on leading conditions, investigate queueing and bandwidth, and scale or tune before the SLO is breached.
Details.errorCorrection: Capacity size is not performance, row count is indirect, and timeout-only detection is late.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More metrics require retention and threshold tuning but improve preventive operations.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Volume size does not show I/O latency or throughput saturation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Row count does not identify block-device queueing.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Waiting for timeouts leaves no response margin.

items.prompt: A data volume grows unpredictably and expansion is currently performed after applications fail. What should improve availability?
constraints: Growth is measurable.
The volume supports expansion.
Data retention cannot be reduced casually.

options.text: Monitor free space and growth, alarm before the safe threshold, automate or rehearse expansion, and validate filesystem growth and performance after the change.
Wait for full capacity so expansion happens only when necessary.
Delete the oldest data automatically without retention approval.
Increase IOPS while leaving capacity unchanged.

feedback.Reason: Capacity exhaustion can cause application failure and needs a leading threshold plus a tested expansion path.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EBS volume and filesystem capacity are separate steps and both must be monitored and expanded safely.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner calculates headroom, expands before exhaustion, checks filesystem visibility, and confirms application behavior.
Details.errorCorrection: Waiting is late, uncontrolled deletion violates retention, and IOPS does not add usable capacity.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Headroom and automation add cost and need safeguards against runaway growth.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Full capacity can already stop writes before expansion completes.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Retention and deletion need business and compliance approval.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: IOPS is performance, not volume capacity.

items.prompt: A production EBS volume must be replaced after corruption while preserving the last known-good data. Which sequence is safest?
constraints: A valid snapshot or backup exists.
The application has a maintenance or failover path.
The replacement must be validated.

options.text: Restore or create a replacement volume from the protected copy, attach and validate it through the application recovery procedure, then cut over with rollback available.
Delete the corrupted volume and create an empty volume with the same name.
Use the newest unverified snapshot because it is always best.
Keep writing to the corrupted volume until it recovers automatically.

feedback.Reason: Replacement recovery should use a known protected copy and a validation and cutover boundary.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Snapshots or backups provide a source for a new volume, but application and filesystem state must be checked before service resumes.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner restores in isolation where possible, validates integrity, switches through the runbook, and retains evidence for rollback.
Details.errorCorrection: An empty volume loses data, newest is not necessarily valid, and continued writes can worsen corruption.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Restore and initialization take time and need an RTO-compatible standby or degraded mode.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Same name does not restore data.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: The newest copy may contain corruption or an incomplete state.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Continued writes can increase data loss and damage.

items.prompt: A team chooses an EBS type from a vendor's maximum IOPS claim without measuring its workload. What review is missing?
constraints: Workload I/O size and concurrency are known or measurable.
Cost and reliability matter.
The instance path may limit results.

options.text: Compare measured IOPS, throughput, latency, burst or sustained behavior, capacity, instance limits, durability, cost, and recovery requirements against the SLO.
Choose the maximum advertised IOPS because more is always better.
Choose the smallest volume regardless of capacity growth.
Use the same EBS type for every workload to simplify operations.

feedback.Reason: EBS selection is a workload and end-to-end path decision, not a maximum-specification contest.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Volume type, size, performance settings, instance bandwidth, durability, cost, and recovery interact.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect benchmarks representative behavior and chooses the smallest configuration that meets the stated performance and reliability objectives.
Details.errorCorrection: Maximum IOPS may overpay or hit another limit, smallest capacity can fail growth, and one type cannot fit every workload.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Standardization reduces operational variety but should not force a performance or reliability mismatch.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Maximum advertised IOPS may not match workload or instance limits.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Capacity growth is a separate requirement that must be planned.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Different workload signals require different volume decisions.

items.prompt: A restored EBS volume must serve a latency-sensitive application immediately after recovery. Which performance action is appropriate?
constraints: The recovery path uses a snapshot.
The application has a strict warm-up requirement.
The team can plan recovery traffic.

options.text: Use an EBS snapshot initialization strategy such as pre-warming the required blocks or using an appropriate fast-restore design, then test recovery latency.
Assume every block has its normal latency as soon as the volume is attached.
Increase the snapshot retention period to improve live read latency.
Restore the snapshot to instance store and treat it as durable.

feedback.Reason: Snapshot-backed volumes can have initialization behavior that must be included in a latency-sensitive recovery design.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EBS snapshot restoration and volume initialization can affect first access to blocks; fast snapshot restore or pre-warming can address the recovery requirement where supported.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner tests the selected restore path with representative reads before declaring the application recovered.
Details.errorCorrection: Attachment alone does not prove every block is warm, retention does not control live initialization, and instance store is ephemeral.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Faster restoration options add cost and have regional, volume, or account constraints that must be checked.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Restored blocks may need initialization before their steady-state performance is observed.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Retention changes recovery copies, not live volume initialization behavior.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Instance store is not durable recovery storage.

items.prompt: A team wants to change a production EBS volume type to improve performance with minimal interruption. What must the runbook include?
constraints: The volume is in use.
The change is supported by the chosen volume types.
Rollback and post-change measurement matter.

options.text: Confirm modification support and limits, protect the data, schedule or observe the change, monitor modification state, and compare application metrics after completion.
Change every volume at once without a backup or canary.
Assume the filesystem will always resize or change type without validation.
Stop all monitoring because the change is managed by AWS.

feedback.Reason: Online EBS modification reduces interruption but does not remove change-management, support, or validation requirements.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EBS volume modification has supported transitions and an in-progress state; performance and filesystem behavior still require observation.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner applies a controlled change, validates health and SLOs, and retains a recovery path if the expected improvement is not achieved.
Details.errorCorrection: A fleet-wide unprotected change increases blast radius, filesystem behavior is separate, and managed service does not eliminate monitoring.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Online changes reduce downtime but can consume operational or performance headroom during modification.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A canary and protected rollback reduce fleet-wide risk.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Filesystem and application validation are still required after a volume change.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Managed operations still need customer-side observability and response.

items.prompt: A volume shows high IOPS but the application still misses its throughput target. Which investigation is most useful?
constraints: The measured IOPS is near the target.
The throughput target is expressed in MiB/s.
The application controls I/O size or concurrency.

options.text: Correlate I/O size, IOPS, throughput, queue depth, latency, and instance bandwidth to determine whether the workload is operation-bound or byte-rate-bound.
Increase IOPS indefinitely without inspecting I/O size.
Reduce capacity because capacity determines throughput in every EBS type.
Move the volume to another Region to reduce local queueing.

feedback.Reason: IOPS and throughput are different measures, and I/O size links the two for the observed workload.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Approximate byte rate depends on operations per second multiplied by bytes per operation and is constrained by volume and instance limits.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect uses representative traffic and metrics to tune the application or provision the correct EBS throughput rather than chasing a single metric.
Details.errorCorrection: More IOPS may not add bytes per second, capacity is not a universal performance control, and another Region adds latency.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Changing I/O size or concurrency can affect CPU, latency, and application semantics and must be tested.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: IOPS alone does not guarantee the required byte throughput.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Capacity-performance coupling depends on the volume type and does not explain every throughput miss.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A Region move changes placement and latency rather than solving the local performance path.

items.prompt: A workload combines multiple EBS volumes in software RAID to increase aggregate throughput. Which trade-off must be explicit?
constraints: The application can use multiple block devices.
Aggregate throughput is required.
The design must recover from a volume failure.

options.text: Validate aggregate performance and instance limits, define volume-level protection and rebuild behavior, and confirm that the recovery objective tolerates the added failure and coordination surface.
Assume RAID makes every volume failure invisible without backups.
Use RAID only to avoid measuring the instance EBS path.
Place all volumes in different Regions for synchronous block writes.

feedback.Reason: Striping can increase parallelism but adds coordination, rebuild, and failure-domain considerations.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Multiple EBS volumes share the EC2 storage path and software RAID changes how failures and recovery are handled.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner benchmarks the aggregate path, protects data with backups or snapshots, and rehearses degraded and rebuild states.
Details.errorCorrection: RAID is not a backup, does not remove instance limits, and EBS block devices are not synchronously written across Regions.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More volumes can increase throughput but also increase configuration, cost, and failure/rebuild complexity.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: RAID redundancy is not a replacement for independent backups and recovery testing.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: The instance path can remain the bottleneck.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Cross-Region synchronous EBS block writes are not provided by the design.
